description: How Netflix’s streaming-scale surge collided with cable’s subscriber collapse—year by year—leading to record streaming dominance and repeated cable profit pain.
youtube_description:
🚨 Cable is dying in slow motion. Meanwhile, Netflix turns the TV industry upside down—one subscriber milestone at a time.

In this chart-race timeline, we compare the rise of streaming scale (Netflix) with the long decline of traditional cable subscribers in the US pay-TV market—then show how competitors like Hulu and Prime Video stack up as the battle shifts.

CHAPTERS
00:00 The moment the shift becomes irreversible
00:45 2013–2014: streaming stops being “niche”
02:10 2015–2016: Netflix crosses into mass adoption
03:35 2018: cable keeps bleeding subscribers
05:05 2020: COVID supercharges watch time and sign-ups
06:20 2022–2023: the market matures—scale wins
07:40 2024–2025: Netflix’s dominance, cable at the bottom

What you’ll see:
• Netflix’s subscriber climb from ~33M (2013) to ~300M (2025)
• Cable’s steep fall across the same era—down to ~26M by 2025
• Hulu and Prime rising as “backup engines” for the streaming category

If you want more “market-turning-point” videos like this, follow and subscribe.

Sources used for the dataset (benchmarked to widely published industry reporting): Netflix quarterly shareholder communications and annual reporting; US pay-TV subscriber counts from major industry trackers (e.g., SNL Kagan / US industry reporting cited widely); Hulu subscriber reporting via company disclosures and industry benchmarks; Amazon Prime household penetration via publicly reported household estimates and major industry measurement summaries.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The TV switch that killed cable wasn’t one event—it was a decade-long subscriber avalanche.

Picture this: in the early 2010s, Netflix is still “the streaming option.” Cable is the default. But the numbers tell you the plot twist arrives slowly… then hits all at once. By 2013, Netflix is at ~33M global subscribers. Two years later it’s ~46M. Then 2015–2017 becomes the acceleration phase: ~65M → ~85M → ~111M. That’s not marketing—it’s momentum.

Meanwhile, cable’s story is the mirror image. In 2010, US pay-TV subscribers sit around ~73M. Each year after, the decline is steady enough to feel survivable—until it isn’t. By 2018, cable is down near ~56M, and by 2019 it’s ~52M. Then 2020 arrives and the market gets brutally clear: cable falls to ~48M while Netflix surges to ~203M. The shift wasn’t just preferences—it became a consumption habit with a compounding effect.

And the “support cast” mattered, too. Hulu grows as a mainstream streaming alternative: ~12M (2015) to ~28M (2018) to ~42M (2020). Amazon Prime Video expands in the background through household penetration: ~55M (2015) to ~80M (2020). By 2022–2023, streaming isn’t a single platform anymore—it’s an ecosystem. Netflix pushes to ~232M (2022) and ~260M (2023), while cable keeps sliding to ~38M (2022) and ~33M (2023).

Fast-forward to 2024–2025: Netflix reaches ~282M then ~300M subscribers, while US cable is around ~29M in 2024 and ~26M by 2025.

So here’s the question: do you think the next “cable moment” will happen to *another* category (sports rights, gaming, or live TV), or is streaming here to stay forever? 💥

Follow for more chart-race breakdowns of the numbers that actually move markets.
facebook_caption:
Cable didn’t lose overnight—it bled subscribers year after year while streaming scaled into the default viewing habit. This timeline comparison tracks Netflix’s global subscriber growth against the US pay-TV subscriber decline.

From 2010 (~73M cable subscribers) onward, cable drops into the 50s by 2018–2019, then accelerates downward during the 2020 transition period. At the same time, Netflix expands from roughly 2013’s ~33M subscribers to ~203M by 2020, then continues scaling through the post-pandemic normalization period—reaching ~300M by 2025.

To capture the broader shift in viewing power, the comparison also includes Hulu’s growth (from ~12M in 2015 to ~55M by 2025) and Prime Video’s expansion through household penetration (from ~55M in 2015 to ~90M by 2025). Together, these trajectories explain why pay-TV’s economics kept deteriorating while streaming reinforced its market position.

Hulu and Prime also climb in the background (Hulu ~12M→~55M, Prime ~55M→~90M). Streaming stops being “an alternative” and becomes the category.
